errors.english: This means wearing clothes in the same manner as those who live at home.
errors.why: The gloss ends with the prohibition itself, 'one should not wear clothes the way one living in a household does', which the English drops.

errors.english: Not of a single color, nor white with a fringe.
errors.why: The root line lists three separate prohibitions (entirely one colour, fringed, white), and the commentary treats 'with fringe' on its own; the English merges fringe and white into one item.

errors.english: summarized this by saying that robes should not be entirely blue or have a fringe
errors.why: mdor mdzad pa most likely means Guṇaprabha put the wording 'entirely blue and fringed' into his (Vinaya)sūtra, not that he summarized it.

note: A faithful commentary rendering. The only slips are in how the root line on robe colours is segmented and one dropped prohibition.

errors.english: just as commanded by the divine order
errors.why: In the drama lha (deva) is the courtly address for the king, so this means 'as commanded by His Majesty', not a divine order.

note: A lively and accurate rendering of the drama scene, with speakers and verses correctly assigned.

errors.english: whether a (Mimamsaka) a follower of the Mimamsa school of Hindu philosophy or another commentator
errors.why: rgyal dpog pa is the proper name Jaimini, the founder of Mīmāṃsā, not a generic Mīmāṃsaka; the same error recurs twice below ('like a (Mimamsaka)', 'is a (Mimamsaka) and so forth').

fix.find: whether a (Mimamsaka) a follower of the Mimamsa school of Hindu philosophy or another commentator

errors.english: Someone who knows objects beyond the senses exists; thus, he himself becomes manifest.
errors.why: The verse concludes that the opponent has thereby admitted for himself that some knower of supersensible things exists; it does not mean that this person 'becomes manifest'.

errors.english: however, if it is through inference [note: term: anumana], then who would fall into this fault?
errors.why: This is the opponent's objection: 'we do not hold that Jaimini etc. know these things by perception, only by inference, so how does this fault apply?' The English garbles it into a question about who incurs the fault.

errors.english: If one relies on scripture for a meaning that is extremely hidden
errors.why: The condition is that, for radically hidden objects, scripture would depend on being confirmed by another non-deceptive pramāṇa; the English loses that dependency.

note: The basic vocabulary of pramāṇa is right, but Jaimini is turned into a generic school label and the opponent's objection about perception versus inference is garbled.

errors.why: yang na introduces an alternative interpretation of the same verse ('Or else'), not an additional point.

note: Bhāviveka's argument about the fire example and the gone, not-gone and being-gone analysis is rendered accurately.
Accurate. The argument on arising and destruction and the objection about worldly entities are rendered faithfully.

errors.why: chos here refers to the dharmas themselves (the ceasing seed and the arising sprout), as the gloss says, not to 'properties'.

note: A sound lemma-by-lemma rendering of the subcommentary on the seed and sprout simultaneity argument.
Faithful rendering of the end of MMK chapter 23 and the opening objection verses of chapter 24, with the verse structure kept.

errors.english: Furthermore, if a doubt were to arise here, consider the case of a (mya ngan) mirage in a desert or wilderness where even a small object appears large.
errors.why: The point is that, although that doubt might arise for the mantra example, no such doubt applies to the desert example where small things look large. The English loses 'there is no doubt here' and wrongly glosses mya ngam (desert) as 'mirage'.

fix.find: Furthermore, if a doubt were to arise here, consider the case of a (mya ngan) mirage in a desert or wilderness where even a small object appears large.
fix.replace: Alternatively, even if that doubt could arise in that case, there is no such doubt in the case where, in deserts, even a small object appears large.

errors.english: those standing to the side whose eyes are not corrupted
errors.why: The onlookers stand beside the illusionists (mig 'khrul mkhan); the English leaves out the illusionists.

note: A good rendering of the Yogācāra argument against real grāhya/grāhaka division, except for the mishandled desert example.

errors.why: 'go is an error for 'gro (the world), as the commentary's gloss 'gro ba 'jig rten 'dzam bu'i gling confirms; it does not mean 'beginning'.

errors.english: Regarding the term perfect, it refers to purity
errors.why: In context 'complete' glosses the Vinaya as complete (tshang ba), i.e. able to carry out motions and formal acts, rather than 'purity'.

errors.english: the word "this" is used for the sake of emphasis
errors.why: The comment is on the restrictive particle (ni, 'only/just') in the line; it has nothing to do with the word 'this'.

note: A solid rendering of the praise of the Vinaya; the main slip is the misread 'beginning' in the verse.

errors.why: lug (Skt. ūrṇāyu) means sheep: the settlements are 'full of sheep'. The note's guess at 'wealth or a specific location' is misleading.

note: The Tibetan verses of the Kalpalatā (colophon, Suprabuddha's wealth and childlessness) are rendered well; the Sanskrit lines are, reasonably, left untranslated.
